title: Ankara Hosts Rival Libyan Factions as Akinci Drone Fires New Supersonic Missile
subhead: Turkey moves to close the Libya file by mediating between its rival camps in Ankara, while a naval test of the UAV-300 air-launched ballistic missile from the Akinci drone extends Ankara's strike reach. July data shows the first current-account surplus in eight months.

sections.heading: Turkey Mediates Rival Libyan Camps in Ankara
sections.body: Turkey hosted talks between rival Libyan factions in Ankara on Sept. 11, per Hürriyet Daily News, the latest step in Ankara's shift from backing one side in Libya's civil war to courting both. The outreach comes after Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan travelled to Benghazi on Aug. 12 for talks with eastern commander Khalifa Haftar, his son Saddam, and senior eastern officials, a day after meeting Tripoli-based PM Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. An Inkstick Media analysis describes this as Ankara's evolving 'One Libya' strategy — keeping its foothold in the west through military presence and commercial ties while building direct links with the east it once fought to repel in 2019.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara is repositioning from proxy-war patron to mediator ahead of any political settlement, hedging its influence across both camps rather than betting on one. It also dovetails with Turkey's energy, reconstruction and arms ambitions in Libya.

sections.heading: Akinci Drone Fires New Supersonic Ballistic Missile in Naval Test
sections.body: Anadolu Agency and Türkiye Today report the Bayraktar Akinci combat drone hit a naval target with the new UAV-300 air-launched supersonic ballistic missile in a test announced Sept. 10-11, with Defence Turkey covering the strike. The platform was earlier described by Defensemirror as gaining a roughly 300 km air-launched ballistic capability. The test extends Turkey's strike reach considerably, giving its flagship drone a standoff weapon that can engage targets far beyond the visual and shorter-range munitions it previously carried.
sections.whyItMatters: A naval-strike capability from a drone armed with a supersonic ballistic missile strengthens Turkey's asymmetric naval and coastal-defense options and reinforces its export pitch just as Bayraktar platforms are being sold to Saudi Arabia and others.

sections.heading: First Current-Account Surplus in Eight Months, but Oil Looms
sections.body: Turkey posted a $36 million current-account surplus in July, its first monthly surplus in eight months, according to Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (CBRT) data cited by Bosphorus News. Economists surveyed by AA Finans had expected a larger surplus of about $582.3 million. Excluding gold and energy the surplus reached $4.97 billion, implying a combined energy and gold deficit of roughly $4.9 billion. The annualized deficit stood near $40.7 billion. Bosphorus News cautions the July data predates this week's oil rally, with Brent now well above the $88 a barrel average assumed in Turkey's new Medium-Term Programme.
sections.whyItMatters: The surplus is a positive sign for the disinflation drive, but it is thin and energy-sensitive — with oil above $100, the external balance could swing back into deficit, complicating the central bank's rate-hold stance.

sections.heading: Turkey-US: F-16 Talk and Likely UNGA Meeting Amid Bank Sanctions
sections.body: Amid the U.S. Treasury blacklisting of a Turkish bank accused of helping launder Iran's oil revenue through an Erdogan ally — a Nordic Monitor report from Sept. 10 — a U.S. lawmaker said there are 'no sanctions' on Turkey and urged F-16 upgrades, according to Hürriyet Daily News (Sept. 11). Türkiye Today reports U.S. congressman Erdogan, Trump are likely to meet at the UN General Assembly this month. The picture is of Washington simultaneously pressuring Ankara on Iran-linked finance while keeping the military relationship on track, with an Erdogan-Trump summit expected in New York.
sections.whyItMatters: The signals are mixed but the direction is toward managed tension: financial enforcement on Iran-linked flows runs parallel to a likely face-to-face Erdogan-Trump meeting, with F-16 and even F-35 questions alive on the agenda.

sections.heading: Turkey and Saudi Arabia Talk After Oil Pipeline Attack
sections.body: Turkey's and Saudi Arabia's foreign ministers discussed regional tensions after attacks on Saudi oil pipelines, with TRT World and Türkiye Today reporting the call (Sept. 11) and Middle East Eye noting the discussion covered the assault on Saudi Arabia. The Bulwark (Sept. 12) describes Saudi Arabia's oil pipeline as hit with multiple attacks. This is the latest ripple of the broader Iran-US conflict and its knock-on pressure on Gulf energy infrastructure, in which Turkey is positioning itself as a regional interlocutor.
sections.whyItMatters: For Turkey, engaging Riyadh amid Gulf infrastructure attacks is both a defensive hedge and a diplomatic opening — it reinforces Turkey's image as a crisis manager while protecting trade and energy interests tied to the Gulf.

sections.heading: Green Power Corridor With Azerbaijan, Georgia, Bulgaria Could Be Signed in November
sections.body: Daily Sabah reports a Turkey-Azerbaijan-Georgia-Bulgaria power-link deal could be signed in November, part of a plan to carry Azerbaijani green electricity to Europe. AzerNews quotes the push to 'connect Eurasia through energy networks,' and trend.az cites Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar framing it as a potential 'TANAP of electricity' for the Turkic world. Anadolu Agency notes the green-electricity push is being advanced at COP31.
sections.whyItMatters: This would extend Turkey's role as an energy transit hub from gas into electricity, deepening ties with Baku and giving Europe a Caspian green-power route at a time of high energy prices and Middle East turmoil.

sections.heading: Defense Industry: MKE-PGZ Air Defense Pact and MKE's Egypt Venture
sections.body: Turkish state-owned firm MKE and Poland's PGZ signed an air-defense cooperation deal, per Anadolu Agency (Sept. 10). This follows breakingdefense.com reporting that MKE launched its first company in Egypt (Sept. 9), extending Turkish defense industrial reach in North Africa. Separately, Daily Sabah (Sept. 10) reports Turkey touting a key command center assisting NATO's preparedness, part of Ankara's ongoing integration with the alliance even as it expands non-NATO partnerships.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkish defense industry is diversifying across NATO (Poland), the Middle East (Egypt) and beyond, leveraging NATO ties for credibility while building independent export channels.

bottomLine: On Sept. 12, Turkey is simultaneously managing a widening diplomatic portfolio — mediating Libya's rival camps, talking to Riyadh after Gulf pipeline attacks, and preparing a likely Erdogan-Trump UNGA meeting — while advancing military and energy projects (the Akinci's UAV-300 missile, a four-country green power corridor) and absorbing a modest July current-account surplus that remains exposed to oil above $100. The through-line is Ankara positioning as a regional crisis manager and transit/industrial hub even as external pressures from the Iran conflict and US sanctions keep pulling at its economy.
sources: Hürriyet Daily News, Bosphorus News (citing CBRT/AA Finans), Anadolu Agency, Türkiye Today, Inkstick Media, Defence Turkey, Defensemirror, TRT World, Middle East Eye, The Bulwark, Nordic Monitor, Daily Sabah, AzerNews, trend.az, breakingdefense.com
